questions.q: A 35-year-old man from rural Bihar presents with a hypopigmented anesthetic patch on his left forearm of 6 months duration. Slit-skin smear shows no bacilli. Nerve biopsy reveals lymphocytic infiltration with well-formed granulomas and no bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) presents with a single well-defined hypopigmented anesthetic patch, negative slit-skin smear (paucibacillary), and histology showing well-formed epithelioid granulomas with lymphocytic infiltration, often eroding the basal layer (Grenz zone absent). Host immunity is high.

questions.q: A 28-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 80 cells/µL) presents with widespread verrucous plaques on the face, trunk, and limbs that have failed to respond to topical treatment for 3 months. KOH preparation shows thick-walled spherical cells with transverse septa (dividing into 4 daughter cells). What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lacazia (formerly Loboa) loboi causes lobomycosis. KOH/histology shows chains of thick-walled yeast cells connected by tubular isthmuses, resembling a string of coins. It causes verrucous, keloid-like plaques. Disseminated/atypical presentations occur in immunocompromised patients.

questions.q: A 45-year-old diabetic man presents with a rapidly progressing necrotic ulcer on the scrotum and perineum for 3 days, with fever and severe pain. Crepitus is felt on palpation. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Immediate wide surgical debridement + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
questions.exp: Fournier's gangrene is a synergistic polymicrobial necrotizing fasciitis of the genitoperineal region. Treatment requires immediate aggressive surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue combined with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering aerobes and anaerobes. Delay in surgery is the main determinant of mortality.

questions.q: A 22-year-old sexually active man presents with a painless indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 10 days. VDRL is reactive at 1:16. Dark-field microscopy shows motile spirochetes. Which of the following correctly describes the causative organism?
opts: Microaerophilic spirochete with 8–14 regular tight coils
questions.exp: Treponema pallidum, the causative agent of syphilis, is a microaerophilic spirochete 6–20 µm long with 8–14 regular coils. It cannot be cultured on artificial media. Dark-field microscopy of exudate from primary chancre is the gold standard for direct diagnosis.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the right T5 dermatome. She reports severe burning pain that began 3 days before the rash. Which antiviral, if started within 72 hours of rash onset, most effectively reduces the risk of post-herpetic neuralgia?
questions.exp: Valacyclovir (prodrug of acyclovir) achieves 3–5× higher bioavailability and is preferred for herpes zoster. The recommended dose is 1000 mg TDS for 7 days. When started within 72 h of rash onset, it reduces duration of acute neuritis and incidence/severity of post-herpetic neuralgia more effectively than standard acyclovir.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with malar erythema, photosensitivity, and oral ulcers for 4 months. ANA is positive at 1:640 (homogeneous pattern). Anti-dsDNA antibodies are strongly positive. Which complement abnormality is classically associated with active disease flare in this condition?
questions.exp: In active SLE, immune complex deposition activates the classical complement pathway, consuming both C3 and C4. Low C3 and low C4 together indicate active disease, particularly lupus nephritis. Monitoring C3/C4 alongside anti-dsDNA titers is used to gauge disease activity and treatment response.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with tense bullae on normal-appearing and erythematous skin, predominantly on flexural areas and thighs, for 3 weeks. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposits along the basement membrane zone. The target antigen is on hemidesmosome. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is the most common autoimmune bullous disorder, predominantly in elderly patients. Autoantibodies target BP180 (type XVII collagen) and BP230 in hemidesmosomes. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ. Bullae are tense (subepidermal cleavage) and Nikolsky sign is negative.

questions.q: A 70-year-old farmer presents with a pearly, translucent papule with rolled borders and central ulceration on the nose for 6 months. On dermoscopy, arborizing telangiectasias are visible. Biopsy shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artifact. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: This is a basal cell carcinoma (BCC) on the nose — a high-risk site for recurrence. Mohs micrographic surgery offers the highest cure rate (>99%) for high-risk BCC by margin-controlled serial excisions. Vismodegib is reserved for metastatic or locally advanced unresectable BCC. Imiquimod is for superficial BCC only.

questions.q: During patch testing, a patient with chronic hand eczema tests positive (++) to p-phenylenediamine (PPD). Which occupation is MOST likely associated with this sensitization?
questions.exp: PPD (para-phenylenediamine) is a primary sensitizer in oxidative hair dyes and is the most common occupational allergen in hairdressers causing allergic contact dermatitis. Cross-reactivity occurs with azo dyes, benzocaine, and sulfonamides. Bricklayers are sensitized to chromate; rubber workers to thiurams/carbamates.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scales on elbows, knees, and scalp. Auspitz sign is positive. Histology would most likely show which characteristic feature?
opts: Parakeratosis with neutrophilic microabscesses (Munro) and elongated rete ridges
Interface dermatitis with vacuolar change at the dermo-epidermal junction
questions.exp: Psoriasis histology is characterized by regular acanthosis with elongated club-shaped rete ridges, parakeratosis, Munro microabscesses (neutrophils in stratum corneum), dilated tortuous capillaries in dermal papillae (explaining Auspitz sign on removal of scale), and thinning of the suprapapillary plate.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with erythema, scaling, and hair loss in a band-like pattern along the frontal hairline for 1 year. Dermoscopy shows peripilar casts, white dots, and loss of follicular openings. Biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltrate at the isthmus and infundibulum with fibrosis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Frontal fibrosing alopecia (FFA) is a variant of lichen planopilaris presenting with progressive recession of the frontal hairline with erythema and scaling. Dermoscopy shows peripilar casts and absent follicular openings. Histology reveals lichenoid lymphocytic infiltrate at the isthmus level with perifollicular fibrosis — a scarring alopecia.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with painful genital ulcers and inguinal lymphadenopathy that has progressed to a fluctuant bubo. Serological testing for syphilis is negative. Aspirate from the bubo cultured on chocolate agar with X and V factors yields a small, Gram-negative coccobacillus. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, a Gram-negative coccobacillus that requires X (hemin) and V (NAD) growth factors. It presents with painful soft ulcers (unlike the painless chancre of syphilis) and tender suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). Chlamydia L1-3 causes LGV with a groove sign, not painful primary ulcer.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman on long-term hydroxychloroquine for discoid lupus develops decreased visual acuity. Ophthalmologic examination reveals a 'bull's eye' maculopathy. What is the mechanism of this toxicity?
opts: Inhibition of melanin synthesis in retinal pigment epithelium
Accumulation of drug in melanin-containing cells, causing photoreceptor damage
Direct toxic effect on corneal endothelium
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine (and chloroquine) binds avidly to melanin in the retinal pigment epithelium, leading to drug accumulation. This disrupts lysosomal function in RPE cells and causes progressive photoreceptor damage, resulting in the classic 'bull's eye' maculopathy. Risk increases with cumulative dose >5 mg/kg/day and duration >5 years.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with multiple hypopigmented macules on the trunk, arms, and face since infancy. Wood's lamp examination shows ivory-white macules with absent melanocytes on biopsy. The lesions are present from birth and are non-progressive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Piebaldism is an autosomal dominant disorder due to KIT gene mutations causing absent melanocytes (amelanotic macules). Key features: present from birth, non-progressive, involves central forehead with white forelock, chest, and mid-extremities — with islands of hyperpigmentation within white patches. Vitiligo is acquired; tuberous sclerosis shows ash leaf macules that are hypopigmented (not amelanotic).

questions.q: A dermatology trainee is performing a punch biopsy for suspected dermatitis herpetiformis. Which site and submission to the laboratory is most appropriate?
opts: From the center of a fresh vesicle; submitted in formalin for H&E
From perilesional normal-appearing skin adjacent to a vesicle; submitted in Michel's medium for DIF
From the edge of an old plaque; submitted in formalin for H&E
From clinically normal distant skin; submitted in saline for electron microscopy
questions.exp: For direct immunofluorescence (DIF) in dermatitis herpetiformis, the biopsy must be taken from perilesional normal-appearing skin (not the vesicle itself, as proteases in it degrade immunoglobulins). The specimen must be submitted in Michel's transport medium (or Zeus medium), which preserves immunoreactants at room temperature for up to 72 hours.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with hardening of skin on the fingers and face, Raynaud's phenomenon, and dysphagia for 6 months. ANA is positive; anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibody is strongly positive. Which pulmonary complication is MOST associated with this antibody profile?
questions.exp: In systemic sclerosis (SSc), anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies are strongly associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc and interstitial lung disease (ILD/pulmonary fibrosis). Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with limited cutaneous SSc and pulmonary arterial hypertension. ILD is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in Scl-70-positive patients.

questions.q: A 24-year-old woman develops a pruritic, erythematous, urticated plaque on her abdomen during the 36th week of pregnancy. It begins within striae gravidarum and spares the umbilicus. Direct immunofluorescence is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP/PUPPP) is the most common specific dermatosis of pregnancy. It begins within striae gravidarum on the abdomen and characteristically spares the periumbilical area. DIF is negative. It is benign, with no fetal risk. Pemphigoid gestationis has positive DIF (linear C3/IgG at BMZ) and periumbilical involvement.

questions.q: A 48-year-old man presents with multiple flesh-colored nodules on the trunk and extremities since childhood, along with 6 café-au-lait spots (each >1.5 cm), axillary freckling, and a Lisch nodule on iris. His son has similar lesions. Which gene is mutated in this condition?
questions.exp: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1, von Recklinghausen disease) is caused by mutations in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17q11.2, encoding neurofibromin (a tumor suppressor/RAS-GTPase activating protein). Diagnostic criteria include ≥6 CALMs >1.5 cm, neurofibromas, axillary/inguinal freckling, Lisch nodules, and first-degree relative with NF1.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with recurrent crops of palpable purpura on the lower limbs for 3 months following an upper respiratory infection. Biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits on DIF. Serum IgA levels are elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) is characterized by palpable purpura (predominantly lower limbs), arthritis, abdominal pain, and renal involvement. DIF shows IgA deposits in vessel walls. It is often triggered by upper respiratory infections. Though more common in children, adult cases tend to be more severe with greater renal involvement.

questions.q: A 19-year-old woman presents with multiple open and closed comedones, papules, and pustules on the face and upper back. She asks about isotretinoin. Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to isotretinoin therapy?
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen (Category X). Pregnancy is an absolute contraindication — it causes major fetal malformations (craniofacial, cardiac, CNS defects). Female patients of childbearing potential must use two forms of contraception and have monthly pregnancy tests (iPLEDGE program in the US). Mild hypertriglyceridemia and depression are relative contraindications requiring monitoring.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with a non-healing ulcer on the dorsum of his right foot for 2 months after a minor injury. He is a rice farmer in West Bengal. Biopsy shows sulfur granules surrounded by neutrophils. Gram stain of granules reveals Gram-positive branching filamentous organisms. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: High-dose penicillin or amoxicillin for 6–12 months
questions.exp: This is actinomycetoma (caused by Actinomyces israelii or Nocardia, bacteria — not fungi). Sulfur granules on histology and Gram-positive branching filaments confirm a bacterial actinomycetoma. Treatment is high-dose penicillin (or amoxicillin-clavulanate) for 6–12 months. Eumycetoma (fungal) is treated with itraconazole; actinomycetoma with antibiotics (penicillin/amoxicillin or co-trimoxazole for Nocardia).

questions.q: A 17-year-old boy presents with perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, and gingivitis. He has been living on a diet of processed foods with very few fresh fruits and vegetables. Which vitamin deficiency explains this presentation?
questions.exp: Scurvy (Vitamin C deficiency) presents with perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew/swan-neck hairs (due to defective keratin), and bleeding gingivitis. Vitamin C is required for hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen synthesis. Deficiency leads to fragile capillaries and impaired wound healing. Pellagra (niacin deficiency) presents with the 3Ds: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia.

questions.q: A 26-year-old woman presents with burning and stinging on sun-exposed areas, notably the nose and cheeks, that worsens in summer. She describes recurring vesicles on the lips after sun exposure. Phototesting shows abnormal response to UVA. Protoporphyrin levels in red blood cells are markedly elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) is caused by ferrochelatase enzyme deficiency (FECH gene mutation). Excess protoporphyrin IX accumulates in RBCs, plasma, and skin. Activated by UVA, it causes burning/stinging, erythema, and waxy scarring on sun-exposed skin. Elevated RBC protoporphyrin is diagnostic. Most photodermatoses do not cause burning on sun exposure; EPP characteristically does.

questions.q: A 33-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 150 cells/µL) presents with deep nodular ulcers on the face and neck with undermined edges and violaceous borders. Skin biopsy shows large intracellular yeast cells within macrophages, 8–15 µm in size, with a narrow neck bud and large capsule. India ink preparation of CSF is positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cryptococcus neoformans causes cryptococcosis, most severe in immunocompromised patients. Skin lesions resemble molluscum contagiosum or ulcers with undermined edges. Histology shows large yeast cells (8–15 µm) with a thick capsule (mucicarmine-positive) and narrow-based budding, within macrophages. India ink preparation of CSF shows the characteristic halo. Treatment: IV liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine.

questions.q: A 65-year-old woman presents with violaceous, flat-topped polygonal papules on the flexor aspects of the wrists and oral white lacy network on the buccal mucosa. Biopsy shows saw-tooth acanthosis, hypergranulosis, and band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the DEJ with civatte bodies. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for extensive cutaneous disease?
questions.exp: Lichen planus with extensive cutaneous involvement requires systemic therapy. Oral prednisolone (0.5–1 mg/kg/day, tapered over 6–8 weeks) is the first-line systemic treatment for extensive lichen planus to achieve rapid control. Topical steroids are used for localized disease. Methotrexate and acitretin are second-line agents for refractory cases.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with a 3-cm pigmented nodule on the left shoulder with irregular borders, variegated color (black, brown, blue-gray), and satellite lesions. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is positive. Breslow thickness is 3.2 mm with ulceration. What is the T and N stage according to AJCC 8th edition?
questions.exp: Per AJCC 8th edition: T4 = Breslow thickness >4 mm (T4a) or >4 mm with ulceration (T4b); T3b = 2.01–4 mm with ulceration. A 3.2 mm Breslow with ulceration = T3b. Wait — T3b is 2–4mm with ulceration. T4b is >4mm with ulceration. 3.2mm with ulceration = T3b. N1a = 1 clinically occult (microscopic) regional node. So T3b N1a is correct.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a painless, non-tender, indurated nodule on his right index finger that developed after handling fish at a fish market. The lesion has been present for 3 weeks and shows a violaceous discoloration. Cultures on enriched media at 30°C yield a Gram-positive rod. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erysipeloid is caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, a Gram-positive rod transmitted from fish, shellfish, or meat. It presents as a well-demarcated, violaceous, non-suppurating, non-pitting edematous plaque on the hands/fingers, typically in fishmongers and butchers. It is painless and self-limiting but responds to penicillin. M. marinum is acid-fast and causes noduloulcerative lesions along lymphatics.

questions.q: A 5-year-old girl presents with bullae and erosions in the mouth, conjunctiva, and skin for 1 week following a febrile illness and use of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Blisters involve >30% of BSA. Nikolsky sign is positive. Skin biopsy shows full-thickness epidermal necrosis with subepidermal bulla. What is this condition?
questions.exp: TEN (Lyell syndrome) involves >30% BSA detachment, mucosal involvement, and full-thickness epidermal necrosis on biopsy. The most common trigger is drugs (sulfonamides, allopurinol, anticonvulsants). SSSS shows intraepidermal cleavage (granular layer), not full-thickness necrosis, and is caused by S. aureus exotoxin — not drug-induced. TEN carries 30–40% mortality.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate develops erythematous, well-defined plaques with silvery scales on the elbows and scalp. She is started on etanercept (anti-TNF-α). After 4 months, she develops new psoriasiform plaques on the palms and soles that were not present before. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.exp: Paradoxical psoriasis is the induction or worsening of psoriasis/psoriasiform lesions by anti-TNF agents (infliximab, etanercept, adalimumab) in patients being treated for other conditions. Despite TNF being a key driver of psoriasis, anti-TNF therapy can paradoxically trigger psoriasis, particularly palmoplantar pustular psoriasis. Mechanisms may involve upregulation of IFN-α by plasmacytoid dendritic cells.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a warty, cauliflower-like growth on the glans penis for 2 years. He is uncircumcised with poor hygiene. Biopsy shows well-differentiated squamous cells invading the stroma in broad pushing fronts, without perineural invasion. HPV in-situ hybridization is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Verrucous carcinoma (giant condyloma of Buschke-Löwenstein) is a locally aggressive, well-differentiated variant of SCC that grows in broad, pushing fronts without destructive stromal invasion or metastasis. It is typically HPV-negative (unlike condyloma acuminatum, which is HPV 6/11 positive). Treatment is surgical excision; it does not respond to radiotherapy (may transform to undifferentiated SCC).

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with hypopigmented macules on the chest and back that fluoresce yellow-green under Wood's lamp. KOH preparation shows short curved hyphae and rounded yeast cells ('spaghetti and meatballs' appearance). He wants a single-dose oral treatment. Which is appropriate?
opts: Ketoconazole 400 mg single dose with exercise (sweating)
questions.exp: Tinea versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (Pityrosporum). For single-dose oral treatment, ketoconazole 400 mg (or 200 mg × 2 days) with exercise to promote sweating is a well-established regimen — sweating delivers the drug to the skin surface. Terbinafine is ineffective against Malassezia (no ergosterol synthesis via squalene epoxidase pathway in this organism). Fluconazole 300 mg weekly for 2 weeks is also used.
